choices.D: Because the officials hacked the accounts only for a legitimate purpose.

questions.explanation: C is correct. The Court said the respondents were mere recipients of what was posted. They did not use unlawful means, because the information was voluntarily given to them by persons with legitimate access. A is wrong because the Court did not say schools are exempt; STC was not faulted only because no violation was shown. B is wrong because minors have privacy rights; the Court even said the photos were personal in nature. D is wrong because no hacking happened. The students showed the photos using their own accounts.

source.part: Our Ruling, STC did not violate petitioners' daughters' right to privacy
source.excerpt: As applied, even assuming that the photos in issue are visible only to the sanctioned students' Facebook friends, respondent STC can hardly be taken to task for the perceived privacy invasion since it was the minors' Facebook friends who showed the pictures to Tigol. Respondents were mere recipients of what were posted. They did not resort to any unlawful means of gathering the information as it was voluntarily given to them by persons who had legitimate access to the said posts. Clearly, the fault, if any, lies with the friends of the minors.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: In Vivares v. St. Theresa's College, which Facebook privacy settings did the Court say might have led to a different result, had their use been proved?

choices.A: 'Public' or 'Friends of Friends'
choices.B: 'Friends' or 'Public'
choices.C: 'Only Me' (or 'Me Only') or 'Custom'
choices.D: 'Friends of Friends' or 'Friends'

questions.explanation: C is correct. The Court said that if it had been proved that access was limited to the uploader through the 'Me Only' setting, or to a select few through the 'Custom' setting, the result may have been different, because the intention to limit access would be more manifest. A, B, and D are wrong because they all include 'Public,' 'Friends of Friends,' or 'Friends,' which the Court said do not clearly keep a post within a zone of privacy. 'Public' is Facebook's default, and even 'Friends' is no assurance that non-friends cannot see the post.

source.part: Our Ruling, STC did not violate petitioners' daughters' right to privacy
source.excerpt: Had it been proved that the access tothe pictures posted were limited to the original uploader, through the "Me Only" privacy setting, or that the user's contact list has been screened to limit access to a select few, through the "Custom" setting, the result may have been different, for in such instances, the intention to limit access to the particular post, instead of being broadcasted to the public at large or all the user's friends en masse, becomes more manifest and palpable.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Jessa, a private individual, takes screenshots of chat messages from Mark's messaging account without his knowledge, and gives them to the prosecutor. Mark is charged with a crime based on the messages. At trial, he moves to exclude them, arguing that under Article III, Section 3 of the Constitution, evidence obtained in violation of the privacy of communication is inadmissible. He also cites Zulueta v. Court of Appeals. Should the motion be granted? Explain, based on Cadajas v. People.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The constitutional exclusionary rule does not apply, because the evidence was obtained by a private individual and not by the State.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Cadajas v. People, the Court held that the Bill of Rights is meant to protect private individuals against government intrusion, so its provisions do not apply between private individuals. The rule on admissibility under Article III must affect only evidence obtained by the State through its agents. The Court called the statement in Zulueta v. Court of Appeals a mere obiter dictum, not a binding precedent. Privacy violations between private individuals are governed by the Civil Code, the Data Privacy Act, and other laws. Admissibility is governed by the Rules on Evidence: relevance, materiality, authentication, and the exclusionary rules.
suggestedAnswer.application: Jessa is a private individual, not a police officer or other agent of the State. So Mark cannot invoke Article III, Section 3 to exclude the screenshots. His reliance on Zulueta fails because Cadajas explained that the pronouncement there was obiter: that petition was about the return of the documents, and the documents were excluded because of the trial court's injunction. Mark's remedy for any privacy violation by Jessa lies under the Civil Code, the Data Privacy Act, or other laws. The screenshots' admissibility will depend on the Rules on Evidence, such as proper authentication.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The motion should be denied on the constitutional ground. The evidence's admissibility is decided under the Rules on Evidence.

keyPoints: The Bill of Rights protects against the State, not against private individuals
The Article III exclusionary rule covers only evidence obtained by the State or its agents
Zulueta's statement on inadmissibility between spouses is obiter dictum
Privacy violations between private persons: Civil Code, Data Privacy Act, other laws
Admissibility: Rules on Evidence (relevance, materiality, authentication, exclusionary rules)

source.part: Our Ruling, on petitioner's right to privacy (the Bill of Rights as protection against the State, and Zulueta as obiter dictum)
source.excerpt: That the Bill of Rights embodied in the Constitution is not meant to be invoked against acts of private individuals finds support in the deliberations of the Constitutional Commission. … While the case of Zulueta v. Court of Appeals (Zulueta) may appear to carve out an exception to the abovementioned rule by recognizing the rule on inadmissibility of evidence between spouses when one obtains evidence in violation of his/her spouse's right to privacy, such a pronouncement is a mere obiter dictum that cannot be considered as a binding precedent. … At any rate, violation of the right to privacy between individuals is properly governed by the provisions of the Civil Code, the Data Privacy Act (DPA), and other pertinent laws, while its admissibility shall be governed by the rules on relevance, materiality, authentication of documents, and the exclusionary rules under the Rules on Evidence. In this case, the photographs and conversations in the Facebook Messenger account that were obtained and used as evidence against petitioner, which he considers as fruit of the poisonous tree, were not obtained through the efforts of the police officers or any agent of the State. Rather, these were obtained by a private individual. Indeed, the rule governing the admissibility of an evidence under Article III of the Constitution must affect only those pieces of evidence obtained by the State through its agents. It is these individuals who can flex government muscles and use government resources for a possible abuse. However, where private individuals are involved, for which their relationship is governed by the New Civil Code, the admissibility of an evidence cannot be determined by the provisions of the Bill of Rights.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Paolo gave his girlfriend the password to his messaging account. Later, she logs in and copies some of his messages, which are used as evidence against him. Paolo says his account is password-protected, so he had a reasonable expectation that no one else could access it, and his right to privacy was violated. Is he correct? Explain, applying Cadajas v. People.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. By voluntarily giving his password to his girlfriend, Paolo limited his reasonable expectation of privacy as to her, so there was no violation.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Cadajas, the Court applied the reasonable expectation of privacy test from Spouses Hing v. Choachuy, Sr. It held that a person who voluntarily gives his password to another, in effect, authorizes that person to access the account. This limits his reasonable expectation of privacy as to that person.
suggestedAnswer.application: Paolo's expectation of privacy came from his account being password-protected. But he does not claim it was hacked or accessed by unauthorized means. He gave his girlfriend the password and took no steps to exclude her. As in Cadajas, his expectation of privacy as to her was limited. The Court also said that once he made the contents available to her, she had the latitude to show others what she could access. In Cadajas, this was true even though the girl was forced by her mother to open the account.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: There was no violation of Paolo's right to privacy.

keyPoints: Reasonable expectation of privacy test (from Hing v. Choachuy)
A password-protected account gives an expectation of privacy
Voluntarily giving the password authorizes the other person's access
No hacking or unauthorized means were used
Conclusion: his expectation of privacy as to that person was limited; no violation

source.part: Our Ruling, on petitioner's right to privacy (application of the reasonable expectation of privacy test)
source.excerpt: Here, petitioner's expectation of privacy emanates from the fact that his Facebook Messenger account is password protected, such that no one can access the same except himself. Petitioner never asserted that his Facebook Messenger account was hacked or the photos were taken from his account through unauthorized means. Rather, the photos were obtained from his account because AAA, to whom he gave his password, had access to it. Considering that he voluntarily gave his password to AAA, he, in effect, has authorized AAA to access the same. He did not even take steps to exclude AAA from gaining access to his account. Having been given authority to access his Facebook Messenger account, petitioner's reasonable expectation of privacy, in so far as AAA is concerned, had been limited. Thus, there is no violation of privacy to speak of.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: During trial, the prosecution formally offers photos taken from the accused's online account. The accused's lawyer makes no objection. After conviction, the accused argues for the first time on appeal that the photos were inadmissible because they violated his right to privacy. Can the appellate court consider the objection? Explain, based on Cadajas v. People.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The objection was waived because it was not made when the evidence was formally offered at trial.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Cadajas, the Court said that to exclude evidence, the objection must be made at the proper time and the grounds must be specified. For documentary evidence, the objection must be made when it is formally offered. A party who fails to object on time is considered to have waived the objection, even if the evidence would have been rejected had it been challenged properly. Also, no question will be considered on appeal unless it was raised in the proceedings below.
suggestedAnswer.application: The accused did not object when the photos were formally offered. Raising the issue for the first time on appeal is barred. In Cadajas, the accused was likewise deemed to have waived his objection, and the photos taken from his Facebook Messenger account were admissible.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The objection is waived, and the photos remain admissible.

keyPoints: An objection to evidence must be made at the proper time, with the grounds specified
For documentary evidence: object when it is formally offered
Failure to object on time means waiver, even if the evidence was inadmissible by nature
Issues cannot be raised for the first time on appeal
Conclusion: the objection is waived

source.part: Our Ruling, on petitioner's right to privacy (failure to object at trial, and issues raised for the first time on appeal)
source.excerpt: Basic is the rule that in order to exclude evidence, the objection to admissibility of evidence must be made at the proper time, and the grounds therefore be specified. Objection to evidence must be made at the time it is formally offered. … When a party failed to interpose a timely objection to evidence at the time they were offered in evidence, such objection shall be considered as waived. This is true even if by its nature the evidence is inadmissible and would have surely been rejected if it had been challenged at the proper time. As a complimentary principle, it is well-settled that no question will be entertained on appeal unless it has been raised in the proceedings below.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: In Cadajas v. People, how did the Court treat the statement in Zulueta v. Court of Appeals that evidence obtained by one spouse in violation of the other's privacy is inadmissible?

choices.A: As a binding precedent that applies to all private individuals
choices.B: As a mere obiter dictum that cannot be considered a binding precedent
choices.C: As overturned because it conflicts with the Data Privacy Act
choices.D: As applicable only to married couples

questions.explanation: B is correct. The Court said the pronouncement in Zulueta is a mere obiter dictum that cannot be considered a binding precedent. One reason is that the Zulueta petition only asked for the return of the documents. Another is that the documents were declared inadmissible because of the trial court's injunction, not because of Article III, Section 3. A is wrong because the Court said it is not binding. C is wrong because the Court did not base its treatment on any conflict with the Data Privacy Act. D is wrong because the Court did not keep it as a rule for spouses; it said the statement is not a binding precedent at all.

source.part: Our Ruling, on petitioner's right to privacy (discussion of Zulueta v. Court of Appeals)
source.excerpt: While the case of Zulueta v. Court of Appeals (Zulueta) may appear to carve out an exception to the abovementioned rule by recognizing the rule on inadmissibility of evidence between spouses when one obtains evidence in violation of his/her spouse's right to privacy, such a pronouncement is a mere obiter dictum that cannot be considered as a binding precedent. This is because the petition brought to the Court in Zulueta simply asked for the return of the documents seized by the wife and thus, pertained to the ownership of the documents therein. Moreover, documents were declared inadmissible because of the injunction order issued by the trial court and not on account of Art. III, Sec. 3 of the Constitution.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: According to Cadajas v. People, the Data Privacy Act allows the processing of data and sensitive personal information when:

choices.A: It is requested by any private person for any reason.
choices.B: It relates to the determination of the criminal liability of a data subject, or is necessary to protect lawful rights and interests in court proceedings.
choices.C: The data subject is a minor.
choices.D: The data was posted on social media.

questions.explanation: B is correct. The Court noted that the DPA allows processing of data and sensitive personal information where it relates to determining a data subject's criminal liability. It also allows it when necessary to protect lawful rights and interests in court proceedings, as in Cadajas, where the evidence was used to establish AAA's claims. A is wrong because there is no blanket permission for any reason. C is wrong because being a minor is not a ground for processing; minors' data deserves more protection, not less. D is wrong because the decision does not say social media posts may be processed freely.

source.part: Our Ruling, on petitioner's right to privacy (Data Privacy Act)
source.excerpt: As further pointed out by Associate Justice Rodil V. Zalameda during the deliberations of this case, the DPA allows the processing of data and sensitive personal information where it relates to the determination of criminal liability of a data subject, such as a violation of R.A. No. 10175 in relation to R.A. No. 9775 and when necessary for the protection of lawful rights and interests of persons in court proceedings, as in this case where the communications and photos sought to be excluded were submitted in evidence to establish AAA's legal claims before the prosecutor's office and the courts.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: In Cadajas v. People, the Court quoted Justice Leonen's separate concurring opinion on the aspects of the right to informational privacy. Which of the following is NOT one of the three aspects listed there?

choices.A: To keep inalienable information to themselves
choices.B: To prevent first disclosure
choices.C: To prevent further dissemination in case the information has already been disclosed
choices.D: To demand payment for any use of one's personal information

questions.explanation: D is correct because it is not one of the aspects. The three listed are: (1) to keep inalienable information to themselves; (2) to prevent first disclosure; and (3) to prevent further dissemination if the information has already been disclosed. The opinion added a possible fourth from the European Union, the right to be forgotten, but not a right to demand payment. A, B, and C are wrong answers because each is one of the three aspects.

source.part: Our Ruling, on petitioner's right to privacy (quoting Justice Leonen's separate concurring opinion)
source.excerpt: Thus, it has the following aspects: (1) to keep inalienable information to themselves; (2) to prevent first disclosure; and (3) to prevent further dissemination in case the information has already been disclosed.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: In Cadajas v. People, which of the following is NOT one of the facts the Court said must be proven to convict for child pornography (R.A. No. 9775, in relation to R.A. No. 10175)?

choices.A: The victim is a child.
choices.B: The victim was induced or coerced to perform in the creation or production of any form of child pornography.
choices.C: The child pornography was performed through visual, audio or written combination thereof by electronic, mechanical, digital, optical, magnetic or any other means.
choices.D: The accused sold or distributed the material to third persons.

questions.explanation: D is correct because selling or distributing is not one of the three facts the Court listed. The Court also explained that the law punishes even mere possession, separately from possession with intent to sell or distribute. A, B, and C are wrong answers because they are exactly the three facts the Court said must be proven.

source.part: Our Ruling, on petitioner's liability
source.excerpt: (1) victim is a child; (2) victim was induced or coerced to perform in the creation or production of any form of child pornography; and (3) child pornography was performed through visual, audio or written combination thereof by electronic, mechanical, digital, optical, magnetic or any other means.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: In Cadajas v. People, what penalty did the Supreme Court impose for child pornography committed through a computer system, and why?

choices.A: Reclusion temporal, because the sweetheart defense lowered the penalty
choices.B: Reclusion perpetua, because R.A. No. 10175 makes the penalty one degree higher than that under R.A. No. 9775
choices.C: A fine only, because the accused was a first-time offender
choices.D: Prision mayor, because the victim was over 12 years old

questions.explanation: B is correct. Sections 4 and 8 of R.A. No. 10175 provide a penalty one degree higher than R.A. No. 9775. One degree higher than reclusion temporal is reclusion perpetua, so the Court modified the CA's penalty to reclusion perpetua, plus a fine of P1,000,000. A is wrong because the Court rejected the sweetheart defense in child pornography, and the penalty was increased, not lowered. C is wrong because the Court imposed reclusion perpetua plus a fine, not a fine only. D is wrong because the decision did not impose prision mayor.

source.part: Our Ruling, discussion of the proper penalty (including the Court's quotation from Disini Jr. v. The Secretary of Justice)
source.excerpt: Sections 4 and 8 of R.A. No. 10175 both explicitly provide that the proper penalty to be imposed for child pornography committed through a computer system should be one degree higher than that provided for in R.A. No. 9775. Under Section 15(b) of R.A. No. 9775, the penalty to be imposed is reclusion temporal in its maximum period and a fine of not less than P1,000,000.00 but not more than P2,000,000.00. … Of course, the law makes the penalty higher by one degree when the crime is committed in cyberspace. But no one can complain since the intensity or duration of penalty is a legislative prerogative and there is rational basis for such higher penalty. The potential for uncontrolled proliferation of a particular piece of child pornography when uploaded in the cyberspace is incalculable. … One degree higher than the penalty of reclusion temporal is the indivisible penalty of reclusion perpetua. Accordingly, the penalty imposed by the CA should be modified to reclusion perpetua as it is in accordance with the provisions and intent of R.A. No. 10175.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A government agency sues several lawyers, together with a businessman, to recover allegedly ill-gotten shares of stock. The lawyers had organized the companies for their clients and, as part of their legal services, held shares as nominees. The agency offers to drop the lawyers from the case if they name the clients for whom they held the shares and turn over the deeds of assignment they executed for those clients. The lawyers refuse, invoking the attorney-client privilege. The agency argues that a client's identity is never privileged. Who is correct? Explain, based on Regala v. Sandiganbayan.

suggestedAnswer.answer: The lawyers are correct. Under the facts, the clients' identities are privileged.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Regala, the Court said the general rule is that a lawyer may not invoke the privilege to refuse to name a client. But there are exceptions. Client identity is privileged: (1) where there is a strong probability that revealing the name would implicate the client in the very activity for which they sought the lawyer's advice; (2) where disclosure would open the client to civil liability; and (3) where the name would furnish the only link needed to form the chain of testimony to convict the client of a crime. In short, the identity is privileged when the client's name has an independent significance, such that disclosure would reveal client confidences.
suggestedAnswer.application: The agency's conditions themselves show that the clients consulted the lawyers, as lawyers, about the corporate set-up of the companies in question, and that the lawyers prepared the deeds of assignment as part of their legal service. Naming the clients would implicate them in the very activity for which they sought advice, and would give the agency the link it needs to build its case. As in Regala, the lawyers were sued only to pressure them into naming their clients. They were being prosecuted solely for services performed as lawyers.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The clients' identities are privileged, and the lawyers may refuse to disclose them. As in Regala, they should be excluded from the case.

keyPoints: General rule: a lawyer may not refuse to reveal a client's identity
Exception: a strong probability that disclosure would implicate the client in the very activity for which advice was sought
Exception: disclosure would open the client to civil liability
Exception: the name is the only link to form the chain of testimony to convict
Summary: privileged when the name has independent significance that would reveal confidences
Conclusion: the lawyers may refuse

source.part: Ruling, Part II, exceptions to the general rule on client identity, and how they apply to the ACCRA lawyers
source.excerpt: Summarizing these exceptions, information relating to the identity of a client may fall within the ambit of the privilege when the client's name itself has an independent significance, such that disclosure would then reveal client confidences. The circumstances involving the engagement of lawyers in the case at bench, therefore, clearly reveal that the instant case falls under at least two exceptions to the general rule. First, disclosure of the alleged client's name would lead to establish said client's connection with the very fact in issue of the case, which is privileged information, because the privilege, as stated earlier, protects the subject matter or the substance (without which there would be not attorney-client relationship). … Petitioners, therefore, have a legitimate fear that identifying their clients would implicate them in the very activity for which legal advice had been sought, i.e., the alleged accumulation of ill-gotten wealth in the aforementioned corporations. Furthermore, under the third main exception, revelation of the client's name would obviously provide the necessary link for the prosecution to build its case, where none otherwise exists.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Distinguish, based on Regala v. Sandiganbayan, between (a) a client who hires a lawyer for advice on how to get around the law in order to commit an illegal act, and (b) a client who thinks he may have already done something illegal and consults a lawyer about it. Is the attorney-client privilege available in each case?

suggestedAnswer.answer: In case (a), the privilege is not available. In case (b), it is available, and the client's name cannot be disclosed if disclosure would lead to evidence not yet in the prosecution's hands.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Regala, the Court said the privilege cannot be invoked or used as a shield for an illegal act, because it is not within the professional character of a lawyer to give advice on the commission of a crime. But where a client thinks he may have previously committed something illegal and consults his lawyer, the privilege applies, for the same policy reasons behind the privilege in general.
suggestedAnswer.application: In case (a), the client seeks help to commit a future illegal act. This falls outside the privilege, since the privilege cannot be invoked for illegal purposes. In case (b), the client seeks advice about a past act. Whether or not the act turns out to be illegal, the prosecution cannot use the lawyer-client relationship to build its case against the client. It must gather its own evidence from other sources.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: There is no privilege for advice on committing a future crime. There is privilege for a client consulting about a possible past wrongdoing.

keyPoints: The privilege cannot be used as a shield for an illegal act
Advising on the commission of a crime is not within a lawyer's professional character
A client consulting about a possible past illegal act is covered
The prosecution cannot use the lawyer-client relationship to build its case
Conclusion: (a) not privileged; (b) privileged

source.part: Ruling, Part II, distinction between seeking advice for illegal purposes and consulting about a past act
source.excerpt: An important distinction must be made between a case where a client takes on the services of an attorney for illicit purposes, seeking advice about how to go around the law for the purpose of committing illegal activities and a case where a client thinks he might have previously committed something illegal and consults his attorney about it. The first case clearly does not fall within the privilege because the same cannot be invoked for purposes illegal. The second case falls within the exception because whether or not the act for which the client sought advice turns out to be illegal, his name cannot be used or disclosed if the disclosure leads to evidence, not yet in the hands of the prosecution, which might lead to possible action against him. These cases may be readily distinguished, because the privilege cannot be invoked or used as a shield for an illegal act, as in the first example; while the prosecution may not have a case against the client in the second example and cannot use the attorney client relationship to build up a case against the latter. The reason for the first rule is that it is not within the professional character of a lawyer to give advice on the commission of a crime. The reason for the second has been stated in the cases above discussed and are founded on the same policy grounds for which the attorney-client privilege, in general, exists.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Five law partners are sued together for the same acts done in the course of their legal work. The government drops one partner from the case because he supposedly promised to reveal his client's identity, but there is no proof he actually did. The other four ask for the same treatment and are refused. Was their right to equal protection violated? Explain, based on Regala v. Sandiganbayan.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes. Dropping one partner but not the others, without a real and substantial distinction between them, violates the equal protection clause.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Regala, the Court explained that the equal protection clause requires the uniform operation of legal norms, so that all persons under similar circumstances are treated the same, both in privileges conferred and liabilities imposed. To treat one person differently, there must be a classification based on substantial distinctions arising from real differences.
suggestedAnswer.application: The partners were similarly situated: all claimed their acts were done in legitimate lawyering. The only reason given for dropping one partner was his promise to name his client. As in Regala, if there is no proof that he actually revealed his client's identity, that promise cannot justify treating him differently. The Court said it is grossly unfair to exempt one similarly situated litigant from prosecution without giving the same exemption to the others.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The four partners' right to equal protection was violated.

keyPoints: Equal protection: persons in similar circumstances must be treated alike, in privileges and liabilities
A different treatment needs a substantial distinction based on real differences
The partners were similarly situated (same claim of legitimate lawyering)
No proof the dropped partner actually revealed his client
Conclusion: equal protection was violated

source.part: Ruling, Part III, equal protection (including the Court's quotation of an earlier decision on the equal protection clause)
source.excerpt: However, respondents failed to show — and absolute nothing exists in the records of the case at bar — that private respondent actually revealed the identity of his client(s) to the PCGG. … What is required under this constitutional guarantee is the uniform operation of legal norms so that all persons under similar circumstances would be accorded the same treatment both in the privileges conferred and the liabilities imposed. … The condition also constitutes a transgression by respondents Sandiganbayan and PCGG of the equal protection clause of the Constitution. It is grossly unfair to exempt one similarly situated litigant from prosecution without allowing the same exemption to the others.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: According to Regala v. Sandiganbayan, which of the following is one of the reasons for the general rule that a lawyer may NOT refuse to reveal a client's identity?

choices.A: The court has a right to know that the client whose privileged information is sought to be protected is flesh and blood.
choices.B: Lawyers are agents of the State and must cooperate with prosecutors.
choices.C: Clients waive confidentiality when they pay legal fees.
choices.D: The privilege covers only communications made in court.

questions.explanation: A is correct. The Court listed it as the first reason for the general rule. The others are: the privilege exists only after a lawyer-client relationship is established; it generally pertains to the subject matter of the relationship; and due process requires that a party know who their opponent is. B is wrong because the Court described a lawyer as an officer of the court owing a fiduciary duty to the client, not an agent of the prosecution. C is wrong because paying fees does not waive confidentiality. D is wrong because the privilege covers communications made in the course of professional employment, not only in court.

source.part: Ruling, Part II, reasons for the general rule on client identity
source.excerpt: First, the court has a right to know that the client whose privileged information is sought to be protected is flesh and blood.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: Under Regala v. Sandiganbayan, which of the following is an exception that makes a client's identity privileged?

choices.A: The client is a public official.
choices.B: Disclosure would open the client to civil liability.
choices.C: The client paid the lawyer in cash.
choices.D: The lawyer and client are related.

Terminal Cab Corporation). A, C, and D are wrong because none of them is one of the exceptions in the decision. choices.B: Where a strong probability exists that revealing the client's name would implicate that client in the very activity for which he sought the lawyer's advice
choices.C: Where the client is a corporation

The Court found that the ACCRA lawyers' case fell under it. A is wrong because never having been charged is not the test. C and D are wrong because they are not exceptions mentioned in the decision.

source.part: Ruling, Part II, first exception to the general rule
source.excerpt: 1) Client identity is privileged where a strong probability exists that revealing the client's name would implicate that client in the very activity for which he sought the lawyer's advice.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: According to Regala v. Sandiganbayan, how must a lawyer treat the attorney-client privilege in order to attain effective representation?

choices.A: As an option the lawyer may use when convenient
choices.B: As a matter of duty and professional responsibility
choices.C: As a right that belongs to the lawyer, not the client
choices.D: As applicable only in criminal cases

questions.explanation: B is correct. The Court said that to attain effective representation, the lawyer must invoke the privilege not as a matter of option but as a matter of duty and professional responsibility. A is the opposite of what the Court said. C is wrong because the privilege protects the client's confidences; the Court described the lawyer's fiduciary duty to the client. D is wrong because Regala itself was a civil case to recover ill-gotten wealth.

source.part: Ruling, Part II, policy considerations behind the privilege
source.excerpt: Encouraging full disclosure to a lawyer by one seeking legal services opens the door to a whole spectrum of legal options which would otherwise be circumscribed by limited information engendered by a fear of disclosure. An effective lawyer-client relationship is largely dependent upon the degree of confidence which exists between lawyer and client which in turn requires a situation which encourages a dynamic and fruitful exchange and flow of information. It necessarily follows that in order to attain effective representation, the lawyer must invoke the privilege not as a matter of option but as a matter of duty and professional responsibility.

questions.prompt: A new government regulation requires all self-employed psychologists, lawyers and doctors to register their appointment books with a tax agency. The books would list only each client's name and the date and time of each appointment, nothing about the consultation itself. The agency says the books will be examined only if a professional is suspected of underpaying taxes, so no one's privacy is harmed. Is the requirement valid? Explain, based on Integrated Bar of the Philippines v. Purisima.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The mandatory registration of appointment books is an unconstitutional intrusion into the right to privacy of the professionals and their clients and patients.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In IBP v. Purisima, the Court held that in deciding a claim of privacy violation, a court must determine whether a person has exhibited a reasonable expectation of privacy and, if so, whether that expectation has been violated by unreasonable government intrusion. Clients and patients have a reasonable expectation of privacy when they set appointments with professionals.
suggestedAnswer.application: People may not want it known that they are consulting a professional. The Court's examples were a battered wife consulting a lawyer, and patients seeing doctors who specialize in particular conditions. Names and dates alone 'paint no picture,' but citing Disini v. Secretary of Justice, the Court said bundling together all of a person's consultations may reveal a pattern of behavior, and that pattern is protected. The agency's claim that the books would be examined only on suspicion does not save the rule. The Court said the mere chance that a person's information may be subject to the State's prying eyes is an unreasonable intrusion. The requirement also violates the confidentiality rules of these professions.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The requirement is void as an unconstitutional intrusion into the right to privacy.

keyPoints: Test: reasonable expectation of privacy, and whether it was violated by unreasonable government intrusion
Clients and patients reasonably expect privacy when setting appointments with professionals
Names and dates together can reveal a pattern of behavior (Disini)
The mere chance of the State's prying eyes is an unreasonable intrusion
It also violates professional confidentiality rules
Conclusion: the requirement is void

source.caseTitle: Integrated Bar of the Philippines v. Purisima
source.part: Decision, Part IV, mandatory registration of appointment books
source.excerpt: Granted, by themselves, names and appointment dates of patients and clients paint no picture. But as Disini teaches, bundling together all the times a person consults with a professional may illustrate a general pattern of behavior, from which information about a person could be revealed, or inferences from information that should have remained private may be drawn. It is this pattern of behavior, which can be extracted from the appointment book, that a person has a reasonable expectation of privacy over and which must be protected. Respondents stress that appointment books need to be registered only and are not automatically subject to the prying eyes of the Bureau of Internal Revenue. They add that the registered appointment books may be viewed only when the self-employed professional is suspected of not paying the correct taxes. Respondents strangely made a case against their own regulation. Nonetheless, the mere chance that a person's information may be subject to the State's prying eyes is an unreasonable intrusion. Considering the risks, this information must not be readily and publicly knowable. That clients and patients may think twice about consulting with professionals, if the government can create a dossier on them based on sensitive information extracted from the appointment book, is more than just an imagined fear.

questions.prompt: Revenue Regulations No. 4-2014 required self-employed professionals to: (a) submit an affidavit of their rates, manner of billing, and the factors they consider in setting fees; (b) register their books of account; (c) register their appointment books; and (d) issue a BIR-registered receipt showing a 100% discount for pro bono services. In Integrated Bar of the Philippines v. Purisima, which of these requirements were upheld, and which were struck down? Why?

suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: A valid regulation (subordinate legislation) must be germane to the purposes of the law it implements. The registration of books of account is supported by the Tax Code. The Court also held that requiring receipts is a valid measure to ascertain the correct taxes. The right to privacy under the Constitution limits government intrusion.
suggestedAnswer.application: (b) Registering books of account is germane to the Tax Code's purpose of monitoring fees and conducting tax audits, so it is valid. (d) Issuing receipts for pro bono services is a valid way to monitor tax compliance. (a) The affidavit of rates and billing serves no legitimate purpose and has no compelling need, so it goes beyond the Tax Code. The Court noted that it does not encroach on the Court's rule-making power or raise serious ethical concerns. (c) Mandatory registration of appointment books is an unconstitutional intrusion into the right to privacy and violates professional confidentiality.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Sections 2(1) and 2(2) of the regulation are void insofar as they require the affidavit and the registration of appointment books. The DOF and BIR were permanently enjoined from implementing those parts.

Pro bono receipts: valid way to monitor tax compliance
Affidavit of rates: void, beyond the Tax Code, no legitimate purpose

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A government agency argues that a lawyer's list of client names is not privileged information, so lawyers may be required to give it to the State. Based on Integrated Bar of the Philippines v. Purisima, is the agency correct? In your answer, explain how the Data Privacy Act treats privileged information.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. Citing Regala v. Sandiganbayan, the Court held that a client's identity falls within the privilege in proper cases.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Attorney-client communication is privileged under Rule 130, Section 24(b) of the Rules on Evidence and Rule 138, Section 20(e) of the Rules of Court. The Code of Professional Responsibility requires lawyers to preserve client confidences. Under Regala, as a general rule a lawyer may not refuse to name a client, but the identity is privileged when the client's name itself has an independent significance, such that disclosure would reveal client confidences. The Data Privacy Act generally prohibits the processing of sensitive personal information and privileged information. Privileged information includes all forms of data that constitute privileged communication under the Rules of Court and other laws. Processing is allowed only in the cases listed in Section 13.
suggestedAnswer.application: The agency's blanket position that client names are never privileged is wrong. The Court said, 'respondents are incorrect in arguing that the client's name is not privileged information.' Requiring lawyers to give client names to the State may force them to violate their duty of confidentiality. Data that is privileged communication is also protected under the Data Privacy Act.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Client names can be privileged in proper cases, so the government cannot simply require lawyers to disclose them.

keyPoints: Attorney-client privilege: Rule 130, Sec. 24(b) and Rule 138, Sec. 20(e)
Regala: client identity is privileged when the name has independent significance
Data Privacy Act generally prohibits processing sensitive personal and privileged information
Privileged information includes data that is privileged communication under the Rules of Court
Conclusion: the agency is wrong; names can be privileged

source.caseTitle: Integrated Bar of the Philippines v. Purisima
source.part: Decision, discussion of the Data Privacy Act and of attorney-client privilege (including the Court's quotation of Regala v. Sandiganbayan)
source.excerpt: The Data Privacy Act generally prohibits "the processing of sensitive personal and privileged information." This includes "any and all forms of data which under the Rules of Court and other pertinent laws constitute privileged communication." … Where the communicated information, which clearly falls within the privilege, would suggest possible criminal activity but there would be not much in the information known to the prosecution which would sustain a charge except that revealing the name of the client would open up other privileged information which would substantiate the prosecution's suspicions, then the client's identity is so inextricably linked to the subject matter itself that it falls within the protection. … Thus, respondents are incorrect in arguing that the client's name is not privileged information. Regala decreed that the client's identity falls within the privilege, in proper cases.

questions.prompt: A member of the House of Representatives asks the Supreme Court to declare a new law on foreign investments unconstitutional because it will supposedly hurt Filipino enterprises. The law's implementing rules have not yet been issued. Based on Garcia v. Executive Secretary, answer these: Is there an actual case or controversy? Is the congressman a proper party? Was the constitutional question raised on time?

suggestedAnswer.answer: There is no actual case or controversy yet, because the implementing rules are absent. The congressman is nevertheless a proper party, and the constitutional question was not raised tardily; it was raised prematurely.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: The decision lists the requisites of a judicial inquiry into a constitutional question: (1) there must be an actual case or controversy; (2) the constitutional question must be raised by a proper party; (3) the constitutional question must be raised at the earliest opportunity; and (4) the resolution of the constitutional question must be necessary to the decision of the case. A controversy must be one that is appropriate or "ripe" for determination, not conjectural or anticipatory. A proper party is one who has sustained or is in danger of sustaining an injury as a result of the act complained of.
suggestedAnswer.application: In Garcia, the Court agreed that there was no actual case or controversy at that point, "particularly because of the absence of the implementing rules that are supposed to carry the Act into effect." Still, the petitioner, as a citizen and taxpayer, and particularly as a member of the House of Representatives, came under the definition of a proper party. The question was not raised tardily but, as the Court said, "prematurely."
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: No ripe controversy yet; proper party; not late but premature.

keyPoints: No actual case or controversy: implementing rules still absent
A controversy must be "ripe", not conjectural or anticipatory
A proper party is one who has sustained or is in danger of sustaining an injury
The petitioner qualified as a citizen, taxpayer and member of the House
The question was raised prematurely, not tardily

source.part: Decision, discussion of the procedural objections (actual case, proper party, timing)
source.excerpt: He also suggests that the constitutional challenge should be rejected outright for noncompliance with the requisites of a judicial inquiry into a constitutional question, to wit: (1) there must be an actual case or controversy; (2) the constitutional question must be raised by a proper party; (3) the constitutional question must be raised at the earliest opportunity; and (4) the resolution of the constitutional question must be necessary to the decision of the case. … Coming first to the procedural objections to the petition, we agree that there is at this point no actual case or controversy, particularly because of the absence of the implementing rules that are supposed to carry the Act into effect. A controversy must be one that is appropriate or "ripe" for determination, not conjectural or anticipatory. We hold, however, that the petitioner, as a citizen and taxpayer, and particularly as a member of the House of Representatives, comes under the definition that a proper party is one who has sustained or is in danger of sustaining an injury as a result of the act complained of. We will also hold that the constitutional question has not been raised tardily but in fact, as just remarked, prematurely.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A law is attacked on broad constitutional grounds: due process, the provisions on nationalism, and economic dependency. The challenger offers strong arguments but no clear and unmistakable showing that the law violates the Constitution. How should the Court rule, and why? Answer based on Garcia v. Executive Secretary.

suggestedAnswer.answer: The Court should reject the challenge and let the law stand, because the challenger failed to show an indubitable ground for declaring it unconstitutional.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: The policy of the courts is to avoid ruling on constitutional questions and to presume that the acts of the political departments are valid in the absence of a clear and unmistakable showing to the contrary. "To doubt is to sustain." The presumption is based on the doctrine of separation of powers, which enjoins upon each department a becoming respect for the acts of the other departments. The theory is that, as the joint act of Congress and the President, a law has been carefully studied and determined to be in accordance with the fundamental law before it was finally enacted.
suggestedAnswer.application: In Garcia, the law was challenged on broad constitutional principles: due process was invoked, the provisions on nationalism were cited, and economic dependency was deplored. In light of the explanations of the Solicitor General and the intervenor, the Court held that the cause of unconstitutionality had not been proved. It was satisfied that the Act does not violate any of the constitutional provisions the petitioner mentioned.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The challenge fails; acts of the political departments are presumed valid, and the petitioner did not overcome the presumption.

keyPoints: Courts avoid ruling on constitutional questions
Acts of the political departments are presumed valid absent a clear and unmistakable showing
"To doubt is to sustain"
Basis: separation of powers (a becoming respect for the other departments)
A law is the joint act of Congress and the President, studied before enactment
The petitioner's broad claims (due process, nationalism, dependency) were not proved

source.part: Decision, discussion of the merits (presumption of validity)
source.excerpt: On the merits, we find that the constitutional challenge must be rejected for failure to show that there is an indubitable ground for it, not to say even a necessity to resolve it. The policy of the courts is to avoid ruling on constitutional questions and to presume that the acts of the political departments are valid in the absence of a clear and unmistakable showing to the contrary. To doubt is to sustain. This presumption is based on the doctrine of separation of powers which enjoins upon each department a becoming respect for the acts of the other departments. The theory is that as the joint act of Congress and the President of the Philippines, a law has been carefully studied and determined to be in accordance with the fundamental law before it was finally enacted. … In the case at bar, the law is challenged on broad constitutional principles and the proposition that the Filipino investor is unduly discriminated against in his own land. Due process is invoked. The provisions on nationalism are cited. Economic dependency is deplored. In the light, however, of the explanation given by the Solicitor General and of the Intervenor in their respective Comments, we hold that the cause of unconstitutionality has not been proved by the petitioner. On the contrary, we are satisfied that the Act does not violate any of the constitutional provisions the petitioner has mentioned.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A legislator argues that a foreign investments law is unwise because it leaves Filipino enterprises at a disadvantage in their own country, and asks the Court to strike it down for that reason. May the Court do so? Where should his objections be heard? Answer based on Garcia v. Executive Secretary.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The Court cannot annul a law simply because it may be unwise or impractical. The objections are better addressed to Congress.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Debatable questions are for the legislature to decide; "the judiciary does not pass upon questions of wisdom, justice or expediency of legislation." In the exercise of judicial power, courts are allowed only "to settle actual controversies involving rights which are legally demandable and enforceable." Under the expanded concept of the political question, the Court may also determine whether there has been a grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction on the part of any branch or instrumentality of the Government.
suggestedAnswer.application: In Garcia, the Court saw "a debate on the wisdom or the efficacy of the Act, but this is a matter on which we are not competent to rule." It found no grave abuse of discretion. It praised the petitioner's civic spirit and zeal but said his views were "expressed in the wrong forum," because "the Court is not a political arena."
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The Court may not strike the law down for being unwise; the petitioner's objections are better heard by Congress, which has the power to rewrite the law.

keyPoints: A debate on the wisdom or efficacy of a law is not for the Court to rule on
Debatable questions are for the legislature to decide
The judiciary does not pass upon the wisdom, justice or expediency of legislation
Courts settle only actual controversies involving legally demandable and enforceable rights
The Court may check only grave abuse of discretion, and none existed here
The remedy is in Congress, which can rewrite the law

source.part: Decision, discussion of the merits (wisdom of the law) and closing paragraph
source.excerpt: What we see here is a debate on the wisdom or the efficacy of the Act, but this is a matter on which we are not competent to rule. As Cooley observed: "Debatable questions are for the legislature to decide. The courts do not sit to resolve the merits of conflicting issues." In Angara v. Electoral Commission, Justice Laurel made it clear that "the judiciary does not pass upon questions of wisdom, justice or expediency of legislation." And fittingly so for in the exercise of judicial power, we are allowed only "to settle actual controversies involving rights which are legally demandable and enforceable," and may not annul an act of the political departments simply because we feel it is unwise or impractical. It is true that, under the expanded concept of the political question, we may now also "determine whether or not there has been a grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction on the part of any branch or instrumentality of the Government." We find, however, that irregularity does not exist in the case at bar. … But his views are expressed in the wrong forum. The Court is not a political arena. His objections to the law are better heard by his colleagues in the Congress of the Philippines, who have the power to rewrite it, if they so please, in the fashion he suggests.

A and C are wrong because the Court said it is not competent to rule on the wisdom or efficacy of the Act and may not annul an act of the political departments simply because it is unwise or impractical. D is wrong because the Court said nothing of the kind about a veto.

source.excerpt: It is true that, under the expanded concept of the political question, we may now also "determine whether or not there has been a grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction on the part of any branch or instrumentality of the Government." We find, however, that irregularity does not exist in the case at bar.
